MP:001.title: Marketing strategy
MP:001.pt: Explain the concept of marketing strategies

scenes.sub: What it is, the two parts it’s built from, and how it shows up on the exam
scenes.cap: A one-minute look at a concept that runs through the Marketing exam.

scenes.text: A business’s plan for reaching its marketing goals by choosing a target market and building a marketing mix to satisfy it.
scenes.cap: Define it first: a strategy is a plan, and it has two parts.

scenes.text: The specific group of customers the business decides to serve.
scenes.cap: No business can serve everyone well, so it chooses whom to focus on.

items.d: What is sold: features, brand name, packaging and services
What customers pay, including discounts and payment terms
Where and how customers get it: stores, websites, delivery
How customers learn about it: ads, social media, personal selling

scenes.cap: These four Ps are the tools the business controls.
Every P is chosen to fit the target market, and the four work together: change one, and the others may need to change too.

rows: Students who want a quick breakfast before class
Next to E117, on the way to class
scenes.cap: Every decision points back to the same group of customers.

a.d: What the business wants to achieve, such as growing its market share from 12% to 15%

b.d: How it will get there: the target market it serves and the marketing mix it uses

scenes.cap: When a question describes a number to reach, that target is a goal, not the strategy itself.

scenes.h: Sorting a decision into the mix
scenes.cap: Ask what the decision changes, and the P usually follows.

FI:238.title: Time value of money
FI:238.pt: Calculate the time value of money

scenes.sub: Why a dollar today is worth more than a dollar later, and how to calculate it
scenes.cap: Have the calculator ready: this concept is mostly math.

scenes.text: The idea that money available now is worth more than the same amount later, because money on hand today can earn interest.
scenes.cap: Define it first: time plus interest changes what money is worth.
Each year’s interest also earns interest, so the growth gets bigger every year.
PV is the amount today, r is the rate per period and n is the number of periods.

scenes.h: Interest more than once a year
scenes.cap: Divide the rate, and multiply the years, by the number of periods per year.

lines: Goal: $5,000 in 5 years at 12%, compounded quarterly
scenes.cap: To find what to deposit today, divide instead of multiply.

items: Compounded once a year instead of quarterly
scenes.cap: Check whether the answer should be larger (future value) or smaller (present value).

scenes.sub: Where investors find reliable facts about a public company
scenes.cap: Before anyone buys a stock, they need trustworthy information. Here is where it comes from.

scenes.text: The facts investors use to judge a company’s stocks and bonds: its financial results, its plans and its major news.
scenes.cap: Public companies must report this information to the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and to their shareholders.

items.d: Yearly document for shareholders: audited statements, a review of the year and future plans
The detailed annual report filed with the SEC
Quarterly report for the first three quarters, with unaudited statements
Current report on major unscheduled events, such as a CEO resigning or a merger

scenes.cap: Match the form to the timing: once a year, once a quarter, or right after big news.

a.d: What the company owns and owes, and the owners’ claim, on one specific date

b.d: Revenues and expenses over a period, such as a year, ending in net income or net loss

scenes.cap: A date points to the balance sheet. A period, and the question “was it profitable?”, points to the income statement.

rows: The section of a company’s website with annual reports, filings and earnings releases
The free online database of every public company’s filings
Stock prices, tables and reporting on company news
scenes.cap: For a company’s own documents, start with its investor relations page.

scenes.h: Match the clue to the source
items: Audited statements and a review of the year, for shareholders
Download the last five annual reports
scenes.cap: Watch the timing words in the question: unexpected, quarterly or yearly.

PR:002.title: Types of promotion
PR:002.pt: Explain the types of promotion (i.e., institutional, product)

scenes.sub: Selling a product, or building the business’s image
scenes.cap: Every ad has a job. The question is whether that job is to sell something specific.

scenes.text: Any communication a business uses to inform, persuade or remind people about its products or about the business itself.
scenes.cap: That last part is the key: some promotion is about the business, not a product.

a.d: Sells specific goods or services by describing features, prices or sales. Example: 30% off all running shoes this weekend.

b.d: Builds the image and goodwill of the business itself, with no product or price. Example: ads about a commitment to sustainable farming.

scenes.cap: If an ad names a product or a price, it is product promotion.

steps: Promote the business, not a product
scenes.cap: Its main goal is a favorable image of the company. The sales come later.

items.d: Shapes how the public feels about the business, often through news coverage
Addresses community issues such as hunger, safety or health, without selling anything

scenes.cap: Both are institutional: neither one tries to sell a product.

items: Employees volunteering at a food pantry; no products or prices
Asking people to donate to a food bank
Shaping the public’s attitudes toward the business
A weekend sale on running shoes
scenes.cap: Look for what the ad is selling. Nothing specific means institutional.

PR:089.title: Direct marketing
PR:089.pt: Explain the nature of direct marketing channels

scenes.sub: Reaching the right people, one at a time, and counting the results
scenes.cap: Direct marketing skips the middle and goes straight to the customer.

scenes.text: Promotion sent straight to chosen individuals, with no intermediaries, that asks for a response the business can measure.
scenes.cap: Three ideas to hold onto: targeted, direct and measurable.

scenes.text: Messages go only to people picked from customer lists or databases: the ones most likely to buy.
scenes.cap: Because each message goes to a qualified prospect, less money is wasted on people who will never buy.

items.d: Postcards, catalogs and letters sent to chosen addresses
Targeted messages that cost little and are easy to measure
Calls to consumers, which must honor the National Do Not Call Registry
Ads that ask people to call, text, scan or order right now

scenes.cap: Every channel asks for an action the business can count.

steps: Print a unique code on each postcard
Count the orders the mailing produced
scenes.cap: This is why startups like email and targeted social media: they are affordable and easy to measure.

a.d: More personal, and questions get answered on the spot, but it costs much more per customer

b.d: Reaches many targeted customers for the cost of printing and postage: less expensive per customer reached

scenes.cap: Personal selling wins on attention. Direct mail wins on cost.

items: Main advantage of direct advertising for a small business
Reaches the people most likely to buy
Checking numbers against the Do Not Call Registry
Magazine ad: text a code for a free sample
scenes.cap: If the response can be traced to the message, think direct marketing.

IM:289.title: Data-collection methods
IM:289.pt: Describe data-collection methods (e.g., observations, mail, diaries, phone, internet, discussion groups, interviews, scanners, tracking tools)

scenes.sub: Asking people, or watching what they do
scenes.cap: Marketing research is only as good as the way the data were collected.

scenes.text: Gathering information for a research question, either by asking people questions or by observing what they actually do.
scenes.cap: Nearly every method falls into one of those two families.

a.d: Surveys and interviews by mail, phone, internet or in person, including focus groups. Shows what people say.

b.d: Watching behavior in person or recording it with devices. Shows what people actually do.

scenes.cap: People don’t always do what they say, which is why observation is valuable.

items.d: A moderator leads a small group discussion. It is a type of interview.
Respondents record their purchases or media use over weeks
Scanners, cameras or tracking tools record behavior
The same set questions asked by mail, phone, internet or in person

scenes.cap: Know which family each method belongs to.

a.d: Focus groups and in-depth interviews: rich reasons and reactions, but from a small part of the market

b.d: Large surveys and scanner data: numbers that can represent a whole market

scenes.cap: Three focus groups of eight teens is 24 people. They can’t speak for every customer.

items: A moderator guides eight people through a discussion
Checkout scanners record items bought together
Households log every snack purchase for four weeks
The limitation of focus group findings
A small part of the market
scenes.cap: Ask: did people tell us, or did we watch them? Then narrow it down.

scenes.sub: The language of business, and the equation underneath it
scenes.cap: Every financial statement starts with the same idea.

scenes.text: Recording, sorting, summarizing and interpreting a business’s financial transactions so people can make decisions.
scenes.cap: Owners, lenders and investors all rely on it.

items.d: What the business owns or is owed: cash, accounts receivable, inventory, equipment
What the business owes others: accounts payable, notes payable
The owner’s claim on the business: assets minus liabilities

scenes.cap: Assets = Liabilities + Owner’s equity. The two sides always balance.
Accounts payable and notes payable are liabilities, so they stay out of the asset total.

a.d: Revenue is recorded when the money comes in, and expenses when they are paid

b.d: Revenue is recorded when it is earned, and expenses when they are incurred, whenever the cash moves

scenes.cap: A landscaper who records revenue on the day it bills the customer is using the accrual basis.

items: Billed today, paid next month, recorded today
Accounts payable or a note payable
scenes.cap: Before adding, sort every item: owned, or owed?

FI:062.title: Time value of money
FI:062.pt: Explain the time value of money

scenes.sub: Why a dollar today beats a dollar next year
scenes.cap: This idea sits underneath interest, loans, savings and investing.

scenes.text: A dollar today is worth more than a dollar in the future, because money you have now can be invested and grow.
scenes.cap: The key word is invested. Time only matters because money can earn interest.

a.d: Still $5,000 when it arrives. The year of interest is lost.

b.d: Can be invested right away. At 4%, it grows to $5,200 by next year.

scenes.cap: Same amount, different value: the payment today is worth more.
Each year’s interest is added to the balance and then earns interest itself.
PV is the amount today, r is the interest rate and n is the number of years.

items: Simple interest: $100 × 3, with no interest on interest
Why money today is worth more
It can be invested to earn interest
scenes.cap: If an answer looks like simple interest, the question probably wants compounding.

scenes.sub: The parts of a check, and how to keep it safe
scenes.cap: Checks are still used for rent, deposits and payroll. Here’s how they work.

scenes.text: A written order telling a bank to pay a stated amount from the writer’s account to a named person or business, the payee.
scenes.cap: Three people are involved: the writer, the bank and the payee.

items.d: The day the check is written
The payee: the person or business receiving the money
Written twice: in numbers in the box and in words on the line
The signature authorizes payment. The memo line is an optional note.

scenes.cap: A check needs the date, the payee, the amount and the signature to be complete.

steps: Start the words at the far left of the line
Draw a line through any space that remains
No room is left to change the amount
scenes.cap: This simple habit keeps anyone from adding words or numbers to raise the amount.

a.d: Writing VOID across the front so the check can’t be used

b.d: Signing the back so the bank can deposit or cash it

scenes.cap: Keisha signs the back of her paycheck before depositing it: she is endorsing it.

items: Signing the back of a check before depositing it
Pay to the order of line
Line drawn through the leftover space
scenes.cap: Front of the check: writing it. Back of the check: endorsing it.

PR:099.title: Ethics in promotion
PR:099.pt: Describe the use of business ethics in promotion

scenes.sub: Honest messages, and the practices that cross the line
scenes.cap: Promotion only works if customers can trust it.

scenes.text: Promotion that is honest, fair and respectful, so customers can trust what a business tells them.
scenes.cap: Some unethical practices are also illegal. All of them cost trust.

items.d: Advertise a bargain, then push customers toward a pricier item
Selling under the guise of research: a “survey” that turns into a sales pitch
Portraying a whole group in an oversimplified, unfair way
Paid product placement that audiences, especially children, may not recognize as an ad

scenes.cap: Each one deceives or disrespects the audience.

a.d: Exaggerated, subjective praise that no one takes literally, such as “the most delicious pizza on the planet.” Generally legal.

b.d: A factual statement that is false or misleading, such as a fake “regular” price. Illegal.

scenes.cap: Puffery can’t be proven true or false. A deceptive claim can be checked, and it fails.

items: A “survey” call turns into an alarm pitch
Cheap laptop advertised, pricier one pushed
Every older adult shown confused by phones
Viewers may not know it’s an ad
scenes.cap: Ask who is being misled, and about what.

SE:062.title: Gathering product information
SE:062.pt: Acquire product information for use in selling

scenes.sub: Where salespeople learn what they need to know
scenes.cap: Customers can tell when a salesperson really knows the product.

scenes.text: What a salesperson needs to know about a product, such as its features, uses, origins, prices and policies, to answer customers accurately.
keys: features, uses, origins, prices and policies
scenes.cap: Today’s customers often ask where and how a product was made, too.

items.d: Using or trying the product yourself: the most firsthand source
Spec sheets, manuals, labels and brochures: best for exact details
People who bought it can share real uses, likes and problems
Sales meetings, product training and supplier representatives

scenes.cap: Each source answers a different kind of question.

scenes.h: Match the need to the source
rows: How the shoes feel on a run
Wearing them on your own runs
Where the restaurant’s beef comes from
How and where menu items are produced
How people really use a blender
scenes.cap: For exact facts, use the manufacturer’s materials, not opinions.
A cruise salesperson studies the brochures so every answer is right.

items: A concierge dines at a new restaurant before recommending it
Using brochures and ads during a sale
Most firsthand knowledge of how shoes perform
scenes.cap: Firsthand means you experienced it yourself.

CM:003.title: Channels of distribution
CM:003.pt: Explain the nature of channels of distribution

scenes.sub: How products, and ownership, get from maker to user
scenes.cap: Every product you buy traveled a path to reach you.

scenes.text: The path a product and its ownership follow from the producer to the final user.
scenes.cap: Every channel starts with the producer and ends with the final user.
Wholesalers and retailers in the middle are called intermediaries.

items.d: Buys in large quantities, takes ownership and resells to retailers or businesses
Buys from producers or wholesalers and sells to final consumers
Helps buy or sell for a commission, but never owns the goods

scenes.cap: The big difference: wholesalers and retailers take title. Agents don’t.

a.d: One or more intermediaries between the producer and the final user

b.d: The producer sells straight to the final user, like handmade soap sold only on the maker’s website

scenes.cap: No middle step means direct.

a.d: Buys for personal or household use

b.d: Buys to run a business or make other products, like a landscaper buying mulch for clients’ yards

scenes.cap: The same mulch can go to either one. What matters is why it’s bought.

items: Finds stores for furniture makers, earns a commission, never owns it
Buys school supplies in bulk and resells them to stores
Large orders through wholesalers help producers…
scenes.cap: Ask two questions: does it take ownership, and whom does it sell to?

BL:133.title: Legal issues in finance
BL:133.pt: Discuss legal considerations in the finance industry

scenes.sub: Fraud schemes, insider trading and the duty to put clients first
scenes.cap: These questions describe a scheme. Your job is to name it.

scenes.text: Deceiving investors to get their money, for example by lying about an investment or trading on secret information.
scenes.cap: The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) enforces the federal laws against it.

items.d: Pays earlier investors with newer investors’ money instead of real profits
Hype a cheap, thinly traded stock with false claims, then sell at the high price
Buying or selling based on important company news that isn’t public yet
Targets a close-knit group, such as a church, using members’ trust in each other

scenes.cap: Promised high returns with almost no risk is the classic warning sign.

scenes.text: Someone legally required to act in the client’s best interest, even when another choice would pay him or her more.
scenes.cap: An advisor who recommends the low-fee fund over the higher-commission one is meeting this duty.

rows: Enforces securities laws, requires accurate disclosure and investigates fraud
Sets monetary policy and supervises banks
scenes.cap: Misleading investors about earnings is an SEC matter.

items: 18% a year, almost no risk, paid with new money
False buyout rumors, then selling the shares
Sold shares before the loss was announced
Few investors checked because they share his faith
scenes.cap: Find the deception, then find whom it targets.

FI:630.title: Statement of changes in equity
FI:630.pt: Explain the nature of statements of changes in equity

scenes.sub: Tracking what the owners’ stake did this year
scenes.cap: This statement connects the income statement to the balance sheet.

scenes.text: A financial statement showing how each owners’ equity account changed during the period, from its beginning balance to its ending balance.
scenes.cap: Think of it as a story about the owners’ stake: where it started, what changed and where it ended.

items.d: Money shareholders invested by buying shares. Changes when shares are issued or repurchased.
Profits kept in the business. Goes up with net income and down with dividends.

scenes.cap: A corporation’s equity comes mainly from these two places.
Dividends are profits paid out to shareholders, so they are subtracted.
Add the profit, subtract what was paid out.

items: Who benefits most from this statement
scenes.cap: Dividends reduce retained earnings. They are not an expense on the income statement.

scenes.sub: What each column tells an investor
scenes.cap: A stock table packs a whole day into one row.

scenes.text: A table of each stock’s trading results for the day, listed by ticker symbol: prices, volume, dividend and key ratios.
keys: prices, volume, dividend and key ratios
scenes.cap: Learn the columns, and the math questions follow.

rows: Short letters that identify the stock, such as TRVB
The price of the first trade of the day
The highest and lowest prices of the day
The price of the last trade of the day
The annual dividend per share. Blank means no cash dividend.
scenes.cap: Comparing open and close shows how the price moved during the day.
Yield is the return from dividends alone, at today’s price.
Investors are paying $15 for every $1 of the company’s yearly earnings.

items: Volume five times normal on a quiet day
Just the $1.44 dividend, not divided by price
scenes.cap: Both ratios divide by something. Check that the answer actually did.

FI:094.title: The income statement
FI:094.pt: Describe the nature of income statements

scenes.sub: Did the business make money this period?
scenes.cap: This is the statement that answers the profit question.

scenes.text: A summary of a business’s revenues and expenses over a period of time, ending in net income or net loss.
scenes.cap: When expenses are greater than revenues, the result is a net loss.

steps: − Cost of goods sold = Gross profit
scenes.cap: There are two subtractions. Gross profit comes first, net income second.
Stopping at $71,500 gives gross profit, not net income.

a.d: A snapshot on one date: assets, liabilities and owners’ equity

b.d: Covers a period: revenues, expenses and the resulting profit or loss

scenes.cap: A loan officer reviews three years of income statements to judge whether profits can cover loan payments.

items: Why a lender reviews past income statements
To judge whether profits can cover payments
scenes.cap: Read to the bottom line: net income is what’s left after every expense.

IM:428.title: Choosing the right research
IM:428.pt: Assess appropriateness of marketing research for the problem/issue (e.g., research methods, sources of information, timeliness of information, etc.)

scenes.sub: Matching the method to the problem
scenes.cap: Good research answers the question asked, in time, at a cost that makes sense.

scenes.text: Research that fits the problem: the right method, a suitable source, current information and a cost the decision can justify.
scenes.cap: Four checks: method, source, timeliness and cost.

a.d: Already gathered for another purpose: quick and cheap, but may be out of date

b.d: Collected now for this problem: relates directly to it, but takes time and money

scenes.cap: An old published study may no longer reflect today’s customers.

scenes.text: A large random sample can stand in for the whole population, so its percentages can be trusted.
scenes.cap: To estimate what percentage of households would buy, use quantitative research with a large random sample.

scenes.h: Match the problem to the research
items: In-depth reactions to a moisturizer’s scent
Percent of households that would buy a meal kit
Decide in two weeks; modest profit at stake
Interviews with 15, then a survey of 2,000
scenes.cap: When time is short and stakes are low, use the data you already have.

items: Main risk of an old published study
The data may be out of date
Key strength of focus groups for a new product
Qualitative and quantitative in one study
scenes.cap: Read the problem for clues about time, money and the kind of answer needed.

OP:015.title: The nature of purchasing
OP:015.pt: Explain the nature and scope of purchasing

scenes.sub: Buying what the business needs to operate
scenes.cap: Every business buys before it sells.

scenes.text: Buying the goods and services a business needs to make its products, run its operations or resell to customers.
scenes.cap: What is bought, and who does the buying, varies by business.

a.d: Merchandise a retailer or wholesaler sells to its own customers

b.d: Raw materials, parts and supplies used to make products or run the business

scenes.cap: A bicycle maker buying steel tubing, paint and tires is doing industrial purchasing.

a.d: One central office buys for every location: bigger orders and more consistency

b.d: Each store, department or region buys for itself, matching local customers’ needs

scenes.cap: A national chain that lets each regional manager choose merchandise is decentralized.
Purchasing doesn’t end with the order: what arrives has to be checked.

items: Regional managers buy for their own stores
A bike maker buys tubing, paint and tires
One office buys for every store
scenes.cap: Find who decides, and what the purchase will be used for.

scenes.sub: The forces behind every price tag
scenes.cap: A price is a decision, and several forces shape it.

scenes.text: Choosing what to charge, based on costs, demand, competition, the business’s objectives and common industry practice.
scenes.cap: Most exam questions describe one of these forces in action.
Change any one of them, and the right price may change too.

a.d: Supply falls short while demand stays high, so prices rise. A frost destroys the strawberry crop at peak season.

b.d: Supply is greater than demand, so prices fall. Too many snow shovels after a mild winter.

scenes.cap: When there’s too much stock, lowering the price helps turn it into cash.

a.d: Buying barely changes when the price changes, often for necessities with few substitutes

b.d: A small price change causes a big change in buying. Raise the car wash price $1, and customers go down the street.

scenes.cap: Close substitutes make demand elastic.
Using the markup that’s standard for gift shops means pricing by industry standards.

items: Raising market share or unit sales
The markup only, not the selling price
scenes.cap: For markup problems, the price is always more than the cost.

scenes.sub: Making decisions people can trust
scenes.cap: Fairness is a skill leaders practice every day.

scenes.text: Treating people by the same standards and basing decisions on facts rather than personal feelings or relationships.
scenes.cap: Being fair doesn’t mean everyone gets the same outcome. It means everyone is judged the same way.

items.d: Judges everyone by the same objective measure
Applies rules the same way every time, to everyone
Hears all sides before deciding
Explains the reason for a decision

scenes.cap: Impartial is the word exams use most.

a.d: Picking the person you like more, or a friend, regardless of performance

b.d: Alana chooses the worker with the stronger performance record

scenes.cap: Same measure for both candidates: that is impartial.

items: Decision based on facts and the same standard
Choosing a friend over a stronger candidate
scenes.cap: Ask what the decision was based on.

scenes.sub: The rules that keep prices competitive and honest
scenes.cap: Businesses set their own prices, within limits.

scenes.text: Federal and state laws that keep businesses competing fairly on price and keep customers from being misled.
scenes.cap: Some laws protect competitors. Others protect customers.

items.d: Competitors agree on the prices they’ll charge instead of competing
Charging competing business buyers different prices for the same goods without a cost reason
Misleading customers about value, such as a fake “regular” price
Pricing below cost to drive competitors out of the market

scenes.cap: Each one either removes competition or misleads buyers.

rows: Bans price fixing and other agreements that limit competition
Limits price discrimination between competing business buyers
Acts against deceptive pricing and advertising
scenes.cap: Price fixing: Sherman. Price discrimination: Robinson-Patman.

items: Three concrete suppliers secretly agree on quotes
Same goods, two competing retailers, different prices
scenes.cap: Agreement among competitors is the giveaway for price fixing.

BL:163.title: The spirit of the law
BL:163.pt: Comply with the spirit and intent of laws and regulations

scenes.sub: Following the law’s words, and its purpose
scenes.cap: A business can be legal and still be wrong.

scenes.text: The purpose a law was written to achieve, such as keeping a river clean.
scenes.cap: Every law has words and a reason for those words.

scenes.h: Two ways to follow a law

a.d: The exact wording. A loophole can follow the words while defeating the purpose.

b.d: The intent behind the words. Responsible businesses honor both.

scenes.cap: Compliance with the letter alone isn’t enough.

rows: Limits what can be dumped into waterways
A method the law’s wording doesn’t cover
Legal, but the river is still harmed
Follows the letter, violates the spirit
scenes.cap: If the law’s purpose is defeated, the spirit is violated.

items: Legal dumping that still harms a river
scenes.cap: Spirit means purpose. Letter means wording.

OP:517.title: Protecting digital assets
OP:517.pt: Comply with strategies for protecting business' digital assets (e.g., website, social media, email, etc.)

scenes.sub: What a business has online, and how to protect it
scenes.cap: A business’s most valuable property may not be something you can touch.

scenes.text: A business’s valuable electronic resources: its website, social media accounts and posts, email lists, logos, apps, domain names and files.
scenes.cap: If it lives on a screen and has value, it’s a digital asset.

a.d: Trucks, forklifts, shelving and other equipment you can touch

b.d: Logo files, a mobile app, a customer email list, the posts on a hotel’s social media accounts

scenes.cap: The exam often hides one digital answer among physical ones.

items.d: List every digital asset and where it’s stored. This is the first step.
Copies kept on a separate, secure system so data can be restored
A password plus a second proof, such as a code sent to a phone
Written rules, such as for laptops, that hold employees accountable

scenes.cap: You can’t protect what you don’t know you have.

steps: Restore from copies on a separate system
scenes.cap: The attack fails because the business still has its data.

items: First step in protecting digital assets
Password plus a code sent to a phone
Reps take client files home on laptops
scenes.cap: Match the threat to the strategy that stops it.

NF:014.title: Monitoring internal records
NF:014.pt: Monitor internal records for business information

scenes.sub: The business information you already have
scenes.cap: Some of the best information a business has is its own.

scenes.text: Information created by a business’s own operations, such as sales reports, inventory records, customer files and financial statements.
scenes.cap: They are accurate, current and free to use.

a.d: Information from outside the business: government data, trade publications, research firms

b.d: Information the business creates itself: point-of-sale reports, inventory counts, customer files

scenes.cap: If the business’s own system produced it, it’s an internal record.

steps: Spot a trend: cookbook sales have doubled
scenes.cap: Regular monitoring turns everyday data into purchasing, staffing and pricing decisions.

items: A manager reviews point-of-sale reports for trends
scenes.cap: Monitoring means checking regularly, not once.

EC:001.title: Economics and economic activities
EC:001.pt: Describe the concepts of economics and economic activities

scenes.sub: Scarce resources, endless wants and the choices in between
scenes.cap: Economics starts with one problem: we can’t have everything.

scenes.text: The study of how people choose to use scarce resources to satisfy their wants.
scenes.cap: Because resources are scarce, every choice involves a trade-off.

a.d: Desires money can’t satisfy, such as friendship or fresh air

b.d: Desires satisfied by goods and services that cost money: food, a haircut, a car

scenes.cap: Economics focuses on economic wants, because meeting them uses scarce resources.

rows: A concert ticket or new running shoes
The running shoes he gave up
scenes.cap: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative you give up.

steps: Production: a farmer grows wheat and a bakery makes bread
Distribution: a truck hauls it to market
Consumption: a family eats the bread
scenes.cap: Consumption is the final goal. Every other activity exists so someone can use the product.

items: Value of the next-best choice given up
The family’s use of the bread
Desires met by things with a monetary value
scenes.cap: Find the choice, and you’ll usually find the opportunity cost.

FI:575.title: Financial globalization
FI:575.pt: Explain the nature and scope of financial globalization

scenes.sub: One connected world of money
scenes.cap: Money now moves across borders in seconds. That brings opportunity and risk.

scenes.text: The linking of financial markets around the world, so money and investments move across borders quickly and easily.
scenes.cap: Two forces drove it: governments opened up, and technology sped up.

items.d: Governments remove limits on foreign investment and on moving money in and out
Internet-based systems move money and trade securities across borders instantly and cheaply

scenes.cap: Electronic trading has done the most to speed it up in recent decades.

a.d: Investing in several countries reduces exposure to any one country’s business cycle

b.d: Trouble in one country’s markets spreads quickly to others

scenes.cap: Because markets are linked, a crisis in one country can pull down its neighbors.

rows: Developing economies with newer financial markets
Fast growth and high potential returns
Markets and governments that may be unstable
scenes.cap: Higher potential return usually comes with higher risk.

items: A currency crisis spreads to neighboring markets
scenes.cap: Spreading out reduces risk. Being linked spreads risk.

EC:017.title: Gross Domestic Product
EC:017.pt: Explain the concept of Gross Domestic Product (GDP)

scenes.sub: The scoreboard for a country’s economy
scenes.cap: GDP is the most widely used measure of a nation’s output.

scenes.text: The total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a year.
scenes.cap: Every phrase in that definition matters on the exam.

items.d: Measured in dollars, at the prices things sell for
Only what’s sold to the end user, so nothing is counted twice
Production inside the borders, no matter who owns the business
A set period of time

scenes.cap: Final is the word students miss most.

rows: A new car sold to a family
Not separately: their value is already in the car’s price
A car built in Michigan by a foreign-owned company
Counted: it was made in the U.S.
A used car resold this year
The car isn’t counted: it was produced in an earlier year
scenes.cap: Intermediate goods are counted once, inside the final product.

items: Why only final goods and services?
Production inside the borders, any owner
scenes.cap: Check each word of the definition against the answer choices.

scenes.sub: Choosing the channel that carries the message
scenes.cap: The right message in the wrong medium reaches the wrong people.

scenes.text: The channels that carry advertising messages to a target audience, such as print, broadcast, direct mail, out-of-home and online media.
scenes.cap: Each medium differs in cost, reach and how precisely it targets.

items.d: Television and radio. TV’s sight, sound and motion make ads memorable, but it is expensive.
Newspapers and magazines
Billboards and transit ads on buses and in train stations
Websites, social media and email. Ad blockers and spam filters can stop them.

scenes.cap: Specialty media adds one more: useful items printed with the business’s name.

scenes.h: Reaching a special interest on TV

a.d: National reach to a broad, general audience

b.d: Specialized channels reach groups with shared interests, such as cooking fans

scenes.cap: A gourmet cooking-tools startup should choose cable.

rows: Ads on city buses and inside train stations
Free leashes printed with the store’s name and number
All the channels that carry ads to an audience
scenes.cap: Specialty items get used again and again, so the message is seen again and again.

items: Ads on and inside public transportation
scenes.cap: Look for where the ad appears. That usually names the medium.

scenes.sub: What borrowing really costs
scenes.cap: Borrowing is never free. Here’s how to find the price.

scenes.text: The total cost of credit: everything paid back above the amount borrowed, including interest and fees.
scenes.cap: Lenders must also state the yearly cost as a percentage, the annual percentage rate (APR).
Multiply the payment by the number of payments, then subtract what was borrowed.

a.d: $6,444.00: everything Jasmine pays back over the 24 months

b.d: $444.00: only the part above the $6,000 she borrowed

scenes.cap: The total repaid is a trap answer. The cost of credit is the extra.

items: Total repaid, not the cost of credit
The yearly cost of credit as a percentage
scenes.cap: Always subtract the amount borrowed.

MP:007.title: The marketing plan
MP:007.pt: Explain the nature of marketing plans

scenes.sub: From where we are to where we want to be
scenes.cap: A marketing plan turns ideas into a set of coordinated actions.

scenes.text: A written document that guides a business’s marketing activities toward specific objectives for a set period of time.
scenes.cap: Its main purpose: everyone works toward the same objectives.

rows: Where the business stands now: strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats
What it wants to achieve, in measurable terms
The target market and marketing mix
Action steps, schedule, people responsible and budget
Measure results against objectives and adjust
scenes.cap: The sections move from analysis to action to measurement.

a.d: Turns strategies into action: who does what, by when, with what budget

b.d: Tracks results, compares them with the objectives and makes adjustments

scenes.cap: Without implementation, a plan stays on paper.

items: Action steps, schedule, people and budget
Main purpose of a written plan
scenes.cap: Match the verbs: analyze, set, choose, act, measure.
